title: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma
tomorrow: before anything existed, what was the very first word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four mahavakyas and how close: the Aitareya's knowing, the Qur'an's jugular vein, near in two different ways. Today the week comes back, and the book ends.

Some things get said twice at the end of a call. Love you, love you. Drive safe, drive safe. The Aitareya Upanishad ends that way too. After prajnanam brahma, it says of the one who knows: with this knowing self, he rose up from this world, gained every wish, and became immortal. Then the last word comes again, all by itself: became.
screen: `LOVE YOU, LOVE YOU.` → `WITH THIS KNOWING SELF.` → `BECAME. BECAME.`

segments.voice: The repeat works like a door pulled firmly shut: this is where the book ends. And this week walked through the whole Aitareya on the way to that door. Food ran from every power, and no single power turned out to be the whole person. A question came twice, who is this one, and pointed past the eye to that by which it sees. Two teachers read the answer two ways: Shankara, one without a second; Ramanuja, Brahman dwelling within the knower. A window opened on gods and elephants and sprouts, all held by knowing. The inside list put desire and will right beside wisdom. And yesterday the Qur'an's jugular vein stood beside the Aitareya's knowing, near in two different ways. Readers differ on who the he of that last line is; some hear it as anyone who knows. What's clear is where the text puts its weight. Not on a new place to go. On the knowing that was there all week, doing the seeing.
screen: `A DOOR PULLED SHUT.` · `FOOD, A QUESTION, TWO READINGS.` · `A WINDOW, A LIST, A NEIGHBOR.` · `THE KNOWING WAS THERE ALL WEEK.` · then, large: `PRAJNANAM BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers what the knowing let in today: one sound, one face, one taste, one thing you learned, one feeling, even a hard one. Fold each finger down slowly. When the hand is closed, rest with whatever knew all five.
The four mahavakyas, and the last of nine days with the first of them: prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman.
Your line: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma, said all the way to the book's last word. A full week, done.

screen: `DAY 1743 COUNTS.` → `THE FOUR MAHAVAKYAS · 9 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WAS THE VERY FIRST WORD?`

howItsDone: Students of the Aitareya read the whole Upanishad with a teacher, ending at its closing line on the one who rises with the knowing self; the great saying prajnanam brahma is then carried into reflection and meditation.

fork.setup: a friend sees a flyer: 'unlock your higher self at a weekend retreat, far from home.' by this week's Aitareya, what's the honest take?

fork.reveal: all week the Aitareya pointed to the knowing by which you see and hear right now. it doesn't send anyone far off to find it.

original.note: Sanskrit amrita, immortal, deathless: in the Aitareya's last sentence, just before 'became' is said twice.

prajnanam brahma.meaning: the knowing is Brahman; one of the great sayings

notes: Block 'the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma', day 9 of 9 (1735–1743), and the week's end (1737–1743). The 2026-10-13 draft gave the three schools' readings; Advaita and Vishishtadvaita now have their own day (1739), so this review recaps the week and lightly teaches the closing line.

The ending: the Sanskrit repeats the verb (amritah samabhavat, samabhavat); the voice renders it 'became immortal. Then the last word comes again: became.' Confirm. The subject 'he' of 3.4 is read by commentators as Vamadeva (from 2.5) or as any knower; the voice says 'readers differ'.
'The repeat works like a door pulled firmly shut' is the writer's image, not a claim about a rule of the text; confirm it's acceptable.
